claims.text: PVD or chemical conversion can produce a uniform 10–20 nm WC coating on tungsten particles.
The WC coating will remain intact during consolidation at approximately 1300°C in a reducing atmosphere if the sintering schedule is optimized.
Variations in sintering conditions can affect the integrity of the WC interphase.
Coating tungsten particles with WC will create a coherent, ultra-thin interphase between tungsten and copper.
The WC interphase will bridge the tungsten and copper phases and ensure a high-quality interface.
The WC interphase will reduce phonon scattering at the W–Cu interface.
The WC interphase will act as a diffusion barrier during high-temperature processing.
Acting as a diffusion barrier will limit deleterious interdiffusion in the W–Cu composite.
WC has hardness and thermal stability that can contribute to the composite's mechanical durability.
The WC interphase will resist irradiation-induced segregation or embrittlement.
The WC-coated W–Cu composite will have more than 10% higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite.
The WC-coated composite will retain mechanical properties similar to those of the uncoated W–Cu composite.
The WC-coated composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to that of the uncoated W–Cu composite.
The predicted improvements will persist at high operating temperatures and under neutron or charged-particle irradiation typical of fusion-reactor joints.
Substantially different processing or service conditions may prevent the predicted enhancements.
The long-term chemical stability of a 10–20 nm WC coating under cyclic thermal stress and irradiation is uncertain.
